title: SQL Day 3 — Filtering & Business Rule Logic
description: Translate stakeholder rules into row-level filters using WHERE, comparisons, Boolean logic, IN, BETWEEN, and LIKE.

topics.title: WHERE — Selecting Relevant Records
topics.business_skill: Filter transaction rows using a business condition.

teaching.teacher:
## WHERE
WHERE keeps only rows that satisfy a condition. Example: SELECT order_id, sales FROM orders WHERE region = 'West';
teaching.explain: WHERE is a row-level filter. FROM identifies the source and WHERE decides which rows remain.
teaching.detailedlearning: Translate phrases such as only, from, belonging to, and transactions with into explicit Boolean conditions.
teaching.expose: Ask which records should remain before writing the SELECT list.
teaching.example: SELECT order_id, customer_name, sales FROM orders WHERE category = 'Technology';
teaching.business_question: The regional sales manager wants all Technology orders. Return order ID, customer name, sales, and region.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT order_id, customer_name, sales, region FROM orders WHERE category = 'Technology';

questions.scenario: The manager is reviewing East-region transactions.
questions.request: Return order ID, customer name, sales, and profit for East-region orders only.

questions.scenario: The manager is investigating Technology transactions.
questions.request: Return order ID, product name, sales, quantity, and profit for Technology orders.

questions.scenario: Operations wants all First Class shipments.
questions.request: Return order ID, customer name, sales, and ship mode for First Class orders.

topics.title: Comparison Operators
topics.business_skill: Translate numeric thresholds into executable rules.

teaching.teacher:
## Comparison operators
Use =, >, <, >=, <=, and <> to express business thresholds. 'At least 1000' means sales >= 1000; 'above 1000' means sales > 1000.
teaching.explain: The operator controls whether the boundary itself is included.
teaching.detailedlearning: Always distinguish above from at least and below from at most. These boundary decisions affect KPI populations.
teaching.expose: Stakeholder thresholds are logic, not just numbers.
teaching.example: SELECT order_id, sales, profit FROM orders WHERE sales >= 1500;
teaching.business_question: The commercial director defines a high-value order as sales of at least 1,500. Return those transactions.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT order_id, sales, profit FROM orders WHERE sales >= 1500;

questions.scenario: A high-value order is defined as at least 1,000 in sales.
questions.request: Return order ID, customer name, and sales for high-value orders.

questions.scenario: Finance is investigating transactions that lost money.
questions.request: Return order ID, category, sales, and profit where profit is below zero.

questions.scenario: The inventory team wants unusually large order quantities.
questions.request: Return order ID, product name, quantity, and sales for orders containing at least 10 units.

teaching.teacher:
## Boolean logic
AND requires every condition to be true. OR requires at least one condition. NOT excludes a condition. Use parentheses when combining OR branches.
teaching.explain: WHERE region='West' AND category='Technology' means both conditions must hold.
teaching.detailedlearning: Translate complex stakeholder rules into logical branches before coding. Example: (West + Technology) OR (East + Furniture).
teaching.expose: The hard part is business logic, not syntax.
teaching.example: SELECT order_id, sales FROM orders WHERE region='West' AND category='Technology';
teaching.business_question: The regional director wants Technology orders sold in the West.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT order_id, customer_name, category, region, sales FROM orders WHERE region = 'West' AND category = 'Technology';

questions.scenario: The manager wants Technology orders from the West.
questions.request: Return order ID, product name, sales, and profit for records matching both conditions.

questions.scenario: The director wants either West Technology or East Furniture transactions.
questions.request: Return order ID, category, region, and sales for either business condition.

questions.scenario: The manager is excluding Furniture while reviewing orders above 500.
questions.request: Return order ID, category, sales, and profit for sales above 500 that are not Furniture.

topics.title: IN & BETWEEN
topics.business_skill: Filter against allowed lists and inclusive ranges.

teaching.teacher:
## IN and BETWEEN
IN checks membership in a list: region IN ('East','West'). BETWEEN checks an inclusive range: sales BETWEEN 500 AND 1500.
teaching.explain: IN replaces repeated OR conditions. BETWEEN includes both endpoints.
teaching.detailedlearning: Use IN for business classifications and BETWEEN for ranges. Remember that BETWEEN 500 AND 1500 includes 500 and 1500.
teaching.expose: Phrases like one of, either, between, and within a range are signals for these operators.
teaching.example: SELECT order_id, region, sales FROM orders WHERE region IN ('East','West');
teaching.business_question: Sales operations is preparing a combined report for East, West, and South. Return order ID, customer name, region, and sales.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT order_id, customer_name, region, sales FROM orders WHERE region IN ('East','West','South');

questions.scenario: The manager is preparing a combined East and West report.
questions.request: Return order ID, customer name, region, and sales for East or West orders.

questions.scenario: Standard-value transactions are defined as sales between 500 and 1500.
questions.request: Return order ID, customer name, sales, and category for orders in this band.

questions.scenario: The team is reviewing three strategic categories.
questions.request: Return order ID, category, product name, and sales for Technology, Furniture, or Office Supplies.
questions.validation: category IN the three requested categories.

teaching.teacher:
## LIKE
LIKE matches text patterns. % means any sequence of characters and _ means exactly one character. Use 'A%' for starts with A and '%Chair%' for contains Chair.
teaching.explain: LIKE is useful when the exact stored text is unknown but a pattern is known.
teaching.detailedlearning: Pattern position matters: starts with, ends with, and contains require different wildcard placement.
teaching.expose: Translate 'starts with', 'ends with', and 'contains' into wildcard patterns.
teaching.example: SELECT order_id, product_name, sales FROM orders WHERE product_name LIKE '%Chair%';
teaching.business_question: The product manager wants transactions for products whose names contain Chair.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT order_id, product_name, category, sales FROM orders WHERE product_name LIKE '%Chair%';

questions.scenario: The team wants customer names beginning with A.
questions.request: Return order ID, customer name, and sales for matching customers.

questions.scenario: The team is investigating chair-related products.
questions.request: Return order ID, product name, category, sales, and profit where product name contains Chair.

questions.scenario: Customer review requires names containing John anywhere in the stored name.
questions.request: Return order ID, customer name, sales, and region for matching records.
